chapters.title: What Is a Plant?
chapters.tease: Every plant descends from one cell that captured a bacterium; together they hold four fifths of Earth's living mass.

chapters.title: The Plant Cell
chapters.tease: The cellulose wall and the water-filled vacuole let plants grow large and firm without muscles or bones.

chapters.title: The Chloroplast
chapters.tease: The chloroplast is a captured bacterium with its own DNA; every plant on Earth inherited it from one ancient cell.

chapters.title: Why Plants Are Green
chapters.tease: Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and lets the green go; satellites read it from orbit.

chapters.title: Extremes of the Kingdom
chapters.tease: From a speck under a millimetre to a single seagrass clone 180 km long, plant bodies span nine orders of magnitude.

chapters.title: Naming Plants
chapters.tease: Two Latin words, anchored to one pressed sheet, let every botanist on Earth be sure they mean the same plant.

chapters.title: The Herbarium
chapters.tease: Nearly 400 million pressed plants, some five centuries old, are botany's archive and its instrument for reading change.

chapters.title: How Many Plants Are There?
chapters.tease: Around 350,000 plant species have names, 2,000 more each year; nearly half of them live on 1.4 per cent of the land.

chapters.title: Plants, Fungi and Algae
chapters.tease: Mushrooms are closer to us than to any plant, and 'algae' is a dozen unrelated lineages; looks deceive.

chapters.title: How a Plant Senses the World
chapters.tease: Without a single nerve, a plant tracks light, gravity, touch, scent, heat and the time of day, and acts on all of them.

chapters.title: The First Photosynthesisers
chapters.tease: Oxygen in the air, iron ore in the ground and the chloroplast in every leaf come from one bacterial invention.

chapters.title: Onto the Land
chapters.tease: Every soil on Earth dates from the moment a scrap of green alga learned to keep its water in.

chapters.title: Mosses, Liverworts and Hornworts
chapters.tease: The smallest land plants built the planet's largest long-term carbon store, one millimetre of peat a year.

chapters.title: Ferns and the Coal Forests
chapters.tease: The coal that powered the industrial age is three hundred million years of swamp forest, burned in two centuries.

chapters.title: The Seed
chapters.tease: An embryo, a packed lunch and a coat: the seed let plants cross deserts and let humans build granaries.

chapters.title: Conifers, Cycads and Ginkgo
chapters.tease: The cone, the resin and the fan-shaped leaf were here before the flower, and they still rule the cold.

chapters.title: The First Flowers
chapters.tease: Darwin called their sudden appearance an abominable mystery; nearly everything on your plate is one of them.

chapters.title: Monocots and Eudicots
chapters.tease: A lawn and the hedge beside it parted company more than 130 million years ago, and you can tell by counting.

chapters.title: The Rise of Grasses
chapters.tease: The youngest great plant family covers a third of the land and supplies more than half of human calories.

chapters.title: Reading the Plant Family Tree
chapters.tease: One gene from 499 species redrew the plant kingdom; the tree is a map of how the green world happened.

chapters.title: The Root
chapters.tease: Roots anchor, drink and store for every land plant, and the hidden half decides the visible half's fate.

chapters.title: Roots and Their Partners
chapters.tease: Nine in ten plants trade sugar for minerals with fungi, and legumes grow their own nitrogen factories.

chapters.title: The Stem
chapters.tease: The stem is scaffold and plumbing at once, and its bundle plan decides whether a plant can ever become a tree.

chapters.title: Wood and Rings
chapters.tease: Wood is a thin sleeve of living cells laying down a dead archive, one ring a year, readable for 12,000 years.

chapters.title: The Leaf
chapters.tease: The leaf is the planet's solar panel, a sandwich a third of a millimetre thick that feeds almost everything.

chapters.title: Stomata
chapters.tease: Every breath of carbon dioxide a plant takes costs it hundreds of molecules of water, paid through pores it can shut.

chapters.title: How Water Climbs a Tree
chapters.tease: A redwood lifts tonnes of water 100 m a day with no pump, by letting its leaves pull on an unbroken thread.

chapters.title: Moving Sugar
chapters.tease: Every potato and every apple was once syrup in a sieve tube, pushed by pressure from a leaf to a sink.

chapters.title: Buds, Shoots and Phyllotaxis
chapters.tease: A dome of cells smaller than a pinhead builds every leaf, and a single rule of spacing writes Fibonacci into the plant.

chapters.title: Hormones and Growth
chapters.tease: Five chemicals made in trace amounts tell a plant where to grow, when to ripen and how tall to be.

chapters.title: The Big Equation
chapters.tease: One equation turns air, water and sunlight into every meal and every breath on Earth.

chapters.title: The Light Reactions
chapters.tease: Two photosystems in series split water, release oxygen and charge the batteries that fix carbon.

chapters.title: The Calvin Cycle
chapters.tease: A slow, abundant enzyme and a three-step cycle are the only road by which carbon enters living things.

chapters.title: C4 and CAM Plants
chapters.tease: By pumping carbon dioxide into a ring of cells or storing it overnight, plants beat RuBisCO's worst flaw.

chapters.title: Plants Breathe Too
chapters.tease: Plants respire in every cell day and night, burning away roughly half the carbon they fix.

chapters.title: Minerals from the Soil
chapters.tease: Seventeen elements dug from the soil, and the scarcest one sets the ceiling on every harvest.

chapters.title: The Nitrogen Problem
chapters.tease: The air is four fifths nitrogen and plants cannot touch it; bacteria, a factory and carnivory are the ways in.

chapters.title: Starch, Sugar and Cellulose
chapters.tease: The same glucose becomes sugar for transport, starch for bread or cellulose for timber, by one bond's twist.

chapters.title: Chemical Defences
chapters.tease: Plants cannot run, so they poison: 200,000 compounds that became our drugs, spices and toxins.

chapters.title: Scents and Signals
chapters.tease: Wounded leaves release scents that summon predators and warn neighbours; cut grass is a cry for help.

chapters.title: Anatomy of a Flower
chapters.tease: Four rings of modified leaves, mapped by three gene classes, are the template for every flower on Earth.

chapters.title: Pollen
chapters.tease: A two-cell package in an indestructible coat: pollen carries sperm to the egg and writes a record in the mud.

chapters.title: Wind, Water and Self
chapters.tease: Grasses, conifers and seagrasses move pollen without animals; selfing is the fallback, and Darwin priced its cost.

chapters.title: Bees and Flowers
chapters.tease: Three in four food crops benefit from animal pollination, and bees do most of that work, most of them wild.

chapters.title: Moths, Birds, Bats and Beetles
chapters.tease: Every flower is a portrait of its pollinator, from a 30-centimetre moth tongue to a gecko's taste for red nectar.

chapters.title: Deceit and Traps
chapters.tease: A third of orchids pay nothing; the fig pays with a nursery. Deception and strict contracts both work.

chapters.title: From Flower to Fruit
chapters.tease: Double fertilisation builds a seed and its food; the ovary around it becomes the fruit we eat.

chapters.title: Seed Dispersal
chapters.tease: A seed that stays home competes with its parent; dispersal decides where forests can be and how fast they move.

chapters.title: Dormancy and Germination
chapters.tease: Seeds carry locks and clocks: cold, fire and smoke decide when a landscape regrows and what a seed bank can save.

chapters.title: Clones and Other Ways
chapters.tease: A plant can copy itself for thousands of years, but only sex lets a lineage change; our crops bet on the copy.

chapters.title: What Makes a Tree
chapters.tease: Trees are not a family but a habit, evolved dozens of times, and three trillion of them shape the planet.

chapters.title: The Oldest and the Biggest
chapters.tease: A pine older than the pyramids, a redwood taller than Big Ben and a 6,000-tonne aspen: the record holders.

chapters.title: How a Forest Grows
chapters.tease: From sterile ash to closed forest within a lifetime: succession is how the green world rebuilds itself.

chapters.title: The Canopy
chapters.tease: The rainforest roof holds most of its leaves, flowers and animals, and we only reached it in the 1980s.

chapters.title: Rainforests
chapters.tease: Six per cent of the land, half of its species, and a forest that recycles its own rain.

chapters.title: Temperate and Boreal Forests
chapters.tease: The taiga is the largest forest on Earth, and the leaf-fall of the north shows up in the planet's breathing.

chapters.title: Fire and Forests
chapters.tease: Many forests need fire to reproduce; a century of putting it out is why today's fires burn so hard.

chapters.title: Trees and Water
chapters.tease: Forests make rain: the Amazon lifts 20 billion tonnes of water a day and waters farms a continent away.

chapters.title: Forests and Carbon
chapters.tease: Forests hold as much carbon as the sky and soak up a third of our emissions, but the sink is weakening.

chapters.title: Living With Trees
chapters.tease: Sustainability was coined by a forester in 1713, and the woods we love most are the ones someone looked after.

chapters.title: Mapping the Green Planet
chapters.tease: Climate, not chance, decides where each plant lives, and satellites now watch the map of vegetation move.

chapters.title: Grasslands and Savannas
chapters.tease: Grasses grow from the base, so fire and grazing that kill trees only trim the grass; the biome that feeds us.

chapters.title: Deserts
chapters.tease: Three ways to beat drought: store water, endure for a millennium, or sleep as seed until the rare rain.

chapters.title: Mountains and the Alpine
chapters.tease: A mountain compresses the world's climates, and its plants crouch, wrap up or grow giant to survive the top.

chapters.title: The Tundra
chapters.tease: Above frozen ground, dwarf trees and sedges race a ten-week summer; the thaw beneath is the climate's loose thread.

chapters.title: Wetlands, Bogs and Swamps
chapters.tease: Waterlogged soil has no oxygen; wetland plants pipe air, lift roots or eat insects, and store a third of soil carbon.

chapters.title: Rivers, Lakes and the Floating World
chapters.tease: Water gives light and moisture but starves plants of gas; aquatic plants are built around air channels.

chapters.title: The Mediterranean Five
chapters.tease: Wet winters and burning summers shaped five scrublands holding a fifth of all plant species on two per cent of land.

chapters.title: Islands
chapters.tease: Isolation turns one arriving seed into a whole flora, and makes herbs into trees; islands are evolution's laboratory.

chapters.title: Plants in the City
chapters.tease: Warmer, drier, trampled and endlessly disturbed, the city is the newest biome, and plants have already evolved for it.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: The First Farmers
chapters.tease: Farming began independently on at least seven continents' worth of soil, and each centre rebuilt the planet.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Wheat
chapters.tease: One in five human calories comes from a grass that stitched three genomes together by accident.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Rice
chapters.tease: Half the world eats rice daily, grown in water by a grass that pipes air to its roots and methane to the sky.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Maize
chapters.tease: Five genes turned a Mexican grass with a dozen stony seeds into the heaviest harvest on Earth.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: The Potato and the Columbian Exchange
chapters.tease: After 1492 the world's crops swapped hemispheres, and a Titicaca tuber fed a quarter of Europe's growth.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Pulses, Roots and Oils
chapters.tease: Protein, starch and fat come from three plant families, and one of them makes its own fertiliser.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Fruit and the Orchard
chapters.tease: Nearly every apple, banana and vine you meet is a clone, kept alive by a 3,000-year-old joint.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Soil, Manure and Rotation
chapters.tease: Soil is a bank account: rotation, manure and chemistry keep it solvent, and the Dust Bowl showed the overdraft.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Breeding Better Plants
chapters.tease: A century of breeding tripled the world's cereal yields and, in doing so, emptied its fields of variety.

chapters.part: Crops and the Story of Farming
chapters.title: Feeding Eight Billion
chapters.tease: Eight billion people eat from a funnel: 390,000 plant species narrow to three grasses and a fifth of a hectare each.

chapters.title: Medicine from Plants
chapters.tease: Plants defend themselves with molecules, and a quarter of our medicines began as a leaf, a bark or a root.

chapters.title: Tea, Coffee and Cocoa
chapters.tease: Caffeine evolved to poison insects; humans turned it into the most widely used stimulant on Earth.

chapters.title: Fibres: Cotton, Linen and Hemp
chapters.tease: Cellulose cell walls clothed humanity for 30,000 years and powered the first industrial revolution.

chapters.title: Timber and Paper
chapters.tease: Wood carried every roof and every written word for most of history, and now promises carbon-storing cities.

chapters.title: Rubber, Resins and Dyes
chapters.tease: Latex, resin and dye are plant defences we borrowed, and the fortunes moved with the seeds.

chapters.title: Spices and Flavour
chapters.tease: Plant chemical weapons that happened to please us drove the trade routes and empires of a thousand years.

chapters.title: Sacred and Symbolic Plants
chapters.tease: Plants carry the meanings we hang on them, and those meanings have protected trees for millennia.

chapters.title: Gardens and Botanic Gardens
chapters.tease: Gardens moved plants out of place for pleasure and profit, and the glass case made it work at sea.

chapters.title: The Plant Hunters
chapters.tease: The people who went to look built the herbaria, gardens and maps that modern botany still rests on.

chapters.title: The Science of Plants
chapters.tease: Each layer of plant science, from Hales's tubes to the genome, answered what the last could only ask.

chapters.title: Deforestation
chapters.tease: Ten million hectares of forest fall each year, mostly old tropical forest; the trees that grow back are not the same.

chapters.title: Invaders
chapters.tease: A plant moved beyond its enemies can swallow a landscape, and the surest cure has been to send the enemies after it.

chapters.title: Diseases and Pests
chapters.tease: Plant diseases travel with trade and find crops with no defences; a monoculture is a bet that nothing new will arrive.

chapters.title: A Changing Climate
chapters.tease: Three centuries of diaries and a thousand years of cherry blossom show plants shifting in time and climbing in space.

chapters.title: Extinction and the Red List
chapters.tease: Two in five plants are threatened and 571 are known extinct since Linnaeus; the Red List is how the danger is measured.

chapters.title: Seed Banks and Living Collections
chapters.tease: Dry a seed, freeze it at minus 18 degrees and it waits a century: the world's crops and wild flora are being banked.

chapters.title: Protecting and Restoring
chapters.tease: Protected areas, the trillion-trees quarrel, the Great Green Wall and a rewilded farm: giving land back to plants.

chapters.title: Gene Editing and New Crops
chapters.tease: From the 1994 tomato to CRISPR and rewired photosynthesis, plant engineering is speeding up what breeders always did.

chapters.title: Growing Differently
chapters.tease: Vertical farms, precision tools, no-till soil and trees among crops: feeding people without exhausting the land.

chapters.title: The Future of the Green Kingdom
chapters.tease: Plants are four fifths of all life by weight and the least known kingdom; what they need from us is room and attention.
